parakeet: The result is that the human function of ritual becomes harder to see, even though that function is often what made the ritual matter in the first place. We become abstracted from nature, seasonality, dependence, and interdependence. Superstition can encourage people to relate to life through metaphysical narrative rather than material reality. Instead of understanding ourselves as embodied, social, ecological beings shaped by time, place, labor, vulnerability, and relationship, we're trained to think in terms of invisible plans, sacred destinies, spiritual warfare, heavenly purpose, and divine symbolism. That abstraction creates distance between people and the actual conditions of life. We learn to see ourselves through myths instead of material reality. And I do not mean myth only in the literary sense. I mean inherited stories that become so dominant that they override observation, history, and human context. People begin to understand their suffering, joy, and future through frameworks that often have more to do with doctrinal loyalty than with reality on the ground. And eventually we lose continuity with the human story. And that may be the deepest loss of all. Because once human practices are enclosed inside supernatural explanation for long enough, people can become strangers to their own inheritance. They no longer see themselves as part of an ongoing human story of adaptation, cooperation, ritualization, memory, creativity, and ultimately survival. They see themselves primarily through a sacred script. That's why my biggest concern with religious superstition is not only what it does to people in the present, it is that it has abstracted our view of ourselves not only in the present, but also in the past and the future. It distorts the past by obscuring what our ancestors were actually doing. It distorts the present by misframing the meaning of our practices now. And it distorts the future by making it harder for people to imagine forms of ritual, community, and meaning that are honest, human, and grounded in reality, even though reality is the home of ritual. That's the cost. Not just confusion, not just misinformation, but alienation from ourselves, one another, and the long human story that made rituals possible in the first place.
